title: Catch Up: Colom Wins Mississippi, Abu Dhabi Ends in a Prisoner Deal, US Jets Leave a UK Base
bluf: This edition covers Tuesday through Thursday because three mornings were missed. AP called Mississippi's Senate race for Democrat Scott Colom, and local outlets report Hyde-Smith conceded. The Abu Dhabi talks ended Wednesday with a deal in principle on a big prisoner swap, but no movement on territory. The US pulled tanker planes out of a British base after an Iranian threat, the clearest sign yet that the war's risk reaches Europe. The House shelved the move to impeach Defense Secretary Hegseth, 211 to 204.

updates.update: Talks moved to Washington, with Qatar's prime minister meeting Trump and Vance. Turkey's spy chief saying a Vance and Rezaei meeting in Doha is planned for next week, which Tasnim denied. Attacks continued: a tanker hit off Oman and an ADNOC ship damaged inside UAE waters on November 10. The fight spread to the Hormuz bypass. It comes with Houthi claims against Saudi pipeline sites. To Europe, where the US moved tankers out of RAF Mildenhall over an Iranian threat.

The Abu Dhabi talks ended November 11 with a deal in principle on a large prisoner swap, expected within two to three weeks. There was no movement on territory. Ukraine says a deal by New Year is possible and wants Europe at the next round.

AP called Mississippi's Senate race for Democrat Scott Colom on November 12, and local outlets report that Hyde-Smith conceded. On November 10 the House shelved Massie's Hegseth impeachment articles. Alaska is still uncalled ahead of the November 18 ranked choice count.

Since November 7 the Taiwan fight has shown up mostly in diplomacy. Beijing still demands that Japan's prime minister retract her Taiwan remark, and Japanese officials now expect no Xi meeting at APEC. Taiwan's election interference arrests continued over the weekend. No fresh daily counts of Chinese military flights for November 10 to 12 could be confirmed.

Lula left on November 9 for COP31 in Turkey and the ASEAN summit in Manila and froze all cabinet and Finance decisions until he returns November 16. Allies now give a timetable: ministers chosen by November 25, full team announced by December 5. A new fight is open over Lula's bid to tie congressional budget amendments to votes.

angles.title: The Iran war is building a Muslim defense bloc without America
angles.argument: Snider argues the Gulf order built on isolating Iran under US protection is coming apart. Gulf states felt exposed when US bases drew Iranian fire. Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed a mutual defense pact, and Egypt and Syria are reportedly weighing joining.
angles.whyNonObvious: A war meant to isolate Tehran may leave Washington, not Iran, outside the region's new security club.
angles.counter: Hawkish analysts, such as those at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, typically argue Gulf states still depend on US weapons and intelligence. To them a new pact is mostly paper.

angles.title: Republicans who deny the war cost them are setting up a repeat
angles.outlet: The American Conservative (W. James Antle III)
angles.argument: Antle argues the Iran war was the main cause of Republican losses, even if it was not the only one. He says party figures blaming candidates or turnout are making excuses. Ignoring the war's cost keeps the party tied to the policy that hurt it.
angles.whyNonObvious: The sharpest case against the war's politics is coming from inside the conservative movement, which shapes the 2028 fight.
angles.counter: Party strategists point to the usual midterm losses for a president's party and to cost of living worries, arguing the war was one factor among many.

angles.title: Trump's own security bureaucracy is limiting his deals
angles.argument: Crooke, a former British diplomat, argues Trump has less control over the Ukraine and Iran talks than he appears to. He points to military planners setting policy through operational plans and to CIA activity against Russia that cut across Trump's outreach. He adds that Moscow and Tehran refuse narrow truces without a wider security deal.
angles.whyNonObvious: It flips the usual picture of an all powerful president and locates the lame duck problem inside his own government.
angles.counter: Mainstream security analysts note Crooke leans partly on secondhand claims and social media posts, and that the president still directly controls strikes and sanctions.

angles.title: China could use climate relocation to win the Pacific
angles.outlet: Lowy Interpreter (Kayly Ober and Debbra Goh, Carnegie Endowment)
angles.argument: As Washington narrows visa routes for Pacific islanders, the authors say China could offer its own climate mobility deals. Beijing has money, flood control technology and experience moving 9.6 million people between 2015 and 2020. It could package this for COP33 in 2028.
angles.whyNonObvious: Climate migration becomes a contest for a dozen Pacific votes at the UN, not just a humanitarian issue.
angles.counter: Human rights groups would say China's mass relocations raise serious consent concerns, and skeptics note Beijing has pledged only $2 million so far.

angles.title: A US base west of the Vistula is a supply hub, not a tripwire
angles.outlet: Breaking Defense reporting, with Brief's reading
angles.argument: Poland will pay up to $4.4 billion for a permanent US base, and all four candidate cities lie in the west of the country. That keeps the base farther from short range Russian strikes and suits moving troops and supplies east. It fits Washington's plan for Europe to carry its own conventional defense.
angles.whyNonObvious: Coverage treats the base as a front line signal, but the likely location points to logistics and survival rather than deterrence by presence.
angles.counter: Polish officials frame any permanent US presence as deterrence wherever it sits. Restraint advocates such as the Quincy Institute argue a new permanent base contradicts the push for Europe to defend itself.

angles.title: The Pentagon is becoming a bank for space and drone firms
angles.argument: The Pentagon's lending office announced close to $1 billion in loans in a few weeks to rocket, radar, drone and chip firms. It wants $20 billion in mandatory money for 2027. The loans aim to fill a launch gap expected after SpaceX stops commercial Falcon 9 flights in 2028.
angles.whyNonObvious: Defense money fights are usually about contracts, but loans let the Pentagon pick industrial winners with far less scrutiny.
angles.counter: Supporters say loans with matching private money are cheaper than grants. Free market critics, such as scholars at the Cato Institute, generally argue government credit crowds out private capital and rewards connected firms.

angles.title: Ukraine is now training NATO, not the other way around
angles.argument: NATO's transformation chief says the alliance uses hidden Ukrainian units and sea drones as the enemy in drills. Ukraine claims it beat NATO navies in all five scenarios at a 2025 exercise. The goal is to force NATO to adapt to cheap drone warfare.
angles.whyNonObvious: Kyiv gains a lasting role inside NATO's training system, a form of leverage that does not depend on membership or on the Abu Dhabi talks.
angles.counter: Pacific focused planners argue Ukraine's lessons come from a land war along a fixed front and may not carry over to fights across long ocean distances.

angles.title: The war did what climate deals could not, but only for now
angles.outlet: Global Carbon Budget, via the New York Times and Carbon Brief
angles.argument: Global fossil emissions are set to fall 0.4% in 2026, mostly because the war drove oil prices up. Oil emissions fell nearly 2% while coal rose. High prices rationed demand rather than clean energy replacing it.
angles.whyNonObvious: COP31 hosts may claim momentum, but the drop rests on a shock that will reverse when peace makes oil cheap.
angles.counter: Researchers quoted by the Guardian say the price spike also sped up the shift to renewables, so part of the drop may last.

stateNarratives.claim: Deputy foreign minister Alexander Grushko said Europeans sit behind the scenes pulling strings, and that EU policy aims to prolong the war as long as possible.
stateNarratives.relatedTo: Abu Dhabi talks and Europe's role
stateNarratives.counterpoint: The joint statement Europe signed with the US and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi backs a negotiated settlement. EU officials say a ceasefire should come first, which Moscow rejects.

stateNarratives.claim: Foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said the Europeans who flew to Abu Dhabi will not take part and can sit in their hotel. He called US coordination with Europe before meeting Russia unpromising.

stateNarratives.counterpoint: Kushner said a lasting deal needs direct talks between Russia and Europe on security. Russia itself wants European security rules on the agenda, which needs Europe present.

underRadar.headline: The Houthis are hitting the pipeline that lets Saudi oil skip Hormuz
underRadar.summary: Saudi Arabia reported a fire on its East West pipeline on November 9, and the Houthis claimed a drone hit on a Yanbu pumping station on November 11. That pipeline is the main way Gulf crude still reaches market while Hormuz is nearly closed.
underRadar.whyUndercovered: Coverage files these as Yemen war news, not as a threat to the one working bypass of the Hormuz blockade.
underRadar.coverage: Middle East Eye and LBCI reported the claims, with little Western wire pickup.

underRadar.headline: An accused assassination planner sits on Russia's peace team
underRadar.summary: FSB counterintelligence chief Dmitry Minaev is on Russia's Abu Dhabi delegation, across the table from Kyrylo Budanov, whom Ukraine says Minaev's unit tried to kill. His department also handles spy arrests of Americans and prisoner handovers.
underRadar.whyUndercovered: Wire coverage listed the headline delegates, not the six experts behind them.

underRadar.headline: Forged court orders and police notices are being used to censor India's internet
underRadar.summary: India's telecom department blocked 129 websites on court orders that appear fake. A teenager also sent forged police notices asking X to block two digital rights groups.
underRadar.whyUndercovered: It surfaced as a short Reuters item and a police case in Delhi, with no national follow up.

underRadar.headline: Congo has handed down 381 death sentences to its own soldiers since early 2025
underRadar.summary: The latest 66 were for fleeing a rebel coalition now led by former president Joseph Kabila.
underRadar.whyUndercovered: Military court rulings in Walikale are reported by Congolese and French radio, not by English wires.

underRadar.headline: Russia's war recruiters shift to Zimbabweans transiting Johannesburg
underRadar.summary: Nine young Zimbabweans were arrested at OR Tambo airport and a hotel under South Africa's anti mercenary law.
underRadar.whyUndercovered: Recruitment arrests in Africa are covered locally and rarely linked to Moscow's deals with Kenya and others.
underRadar.coverage: AllAfrica roundup and South African outlets.

underRadar.headline: US refiners skipped maintenance to keep fuel flowing during the war
underRadar.summary: Many US refineries put off routine maintenance this year to keep supply steady, and that work is coming due.
underRadar.whyUndercovered: Coverage focused on gas dropping below $4, not on what keeps it there.

conspiracies.claim: Governments are timing alerts and drills to prepare people for a planned crisis, and the Nov 17 national alert test is the next step.
conspiracies.status: The test is real and announced. A planned crisis behind it is unproven.
conspiracies.harm: Moderate. It can push people to disable phone alerts, which weakens real warnings, and it feeds panic buying.
conspiracies.whereSpreading: Corbett Report, NaturalNews, ZeroHedge, prepper and collapse sites, Telegram channels
conspiracies.origin: Corbett's Nov 4 episode on emergency warnings around the world, a wave of government stockpiling advice abroad, and ZeroHedge's unexplained Doomsday Plane flight story
conspiracies.whyBelieved: Several real signals arrived at once. There is a war and stockpiling advice in many countries. There is also a Pentagon plan for bases to run 90 days off the grid, and a national alert test. People read clusters as plans.
conspiracies.caseFor: The events are real and close together. Officials rarely explain why readiness drills cluster, and the E-4B flight had no public explanation.
conspiracies.caseAgainst: FEMA and the FCC announced the Nov 17 test in September with a Dec 3 backup date. Nationwide tests run every year or two. NaturalNews's own article body calls it a routine drill needing no public action, and ZeroHedge notes E-4B jets fly routine training missions.
conspiracies.unknowns: Why the E-4B flew east. Whether any agency is preparing for a specific event tied to the Iran war.
conspiracies.watch: The Nov 17 test, posts claiming alerts were used to track phones, and any second unexplained E-4B or TACAMO flight.
conspiracies.relatedTo: Doomsday date Nov 13, Iran war, Pentagon grid survival plan
conspiracies.audience: Preppers, libertarians, older right leaning readers, some wellness audiences
conspiracies.forumChatter: Not measured. NaturalNews files the test under a Collapse section with crisis headlines in the sidebar.

conspiracies.claim: Jensen Huang was compromised by a Chinese intelligence honey trap, and Trump shielded him to protect China trade.
conspiracies.status: Affair admitted. Spy role not confirmed by the Justice Department. New since Nov 8: Huang is out as CEO.
conspiracies.harm: Moderate. It can fuel suspicion of Chinese American executives and staff in tech.
conspiracies.whereSpreading: Right and left alike: Epoch Times and MAGA influencers stress Chinese espionage, liberal outlets stress that Trump ignored a warning.
conspiracies.origin: Reports by the Wall Street Journal and New York Times citing US intelligence officials, after Huang admitted the affair to staff
conspiracies.whyBelieved: It joins two widely held fears, Chinese spying and Trump trading security for deals, so both camps find a villain.
conspiracies.caseFor: Huang admitted the affair. Alice Huang is a former Chinese state TV reporter at a firm that bought billions in Nvidia chips and faces a criminal probe. The Times says Trump was briefed and did not act.
conspiracies.caseAgainst: Todd Blanche of the Justice Department says the spy claim is not confirmed. China denies it. No evidence shows Nvidia steered the Megaspeed case.
conspiracies.unknowns: What intelligence officials actually found, what if anything was passed to Beijing, and why Huang left.
conspiracies.watch: Any indictment in the Megaspeed case, congressional letters from the new Democratic majority, and Trump's China trip plans.
conspiracies.relatedTo: AI chip export controls, Trump and China trade talks
conspiracies.audience: Broad. China hawks on the right, Trump critics on the left, tech investors

conspiracies.claim: The Israel lobby is secretly programming AI chatbots to push pro Israel narratives and bury criticism.
conspiracies.status: Lobbying of AI firms is publicly acknowledged. Secret programming of outputs is unproven.
conspiracies.harm: Moderate. It can slide into antisemitic ideas about Jewish control of technology.
conspiracies.whereSpreading: Caitlin Johnstone via Consortium News, pro Palestinian accounts, left alternative media
conspiracies.origin: ADL chief Jonathan Greenblatt's October remarks that his group tests AI models, and an academic's June talk at an American Jewish Committee event
conspiracies.whyBelieved: Advocacy groups said openly that they press AI labs, and many users already see chatbots hedge on Gaza.
conspiracies.caseFor: Greenblatt and Maya Ackerman described this work on the record. AI labs do consult outside groups when tuning safety rules.
conspiracies.caseAgainst: Labs consult many advocacy groups across issues. Johnstone shows no specific output changed at a lobby's request, and testing for hate speech is not the same as steering opinion on a war.
conspiracies.unknowns: Which outside groups each lab consults and how much weight their input carries.
conspiracies.watch: Whether any AI company publishes its list of outside safety testers, and whether this spreads from the left into right wing anti Israel circles.
conspiracies.relatedTo: Israel aid fight, Big Tech moderation debates
conspiracies.audience: Popular on the left and with pro Palestinian activists, with some crossover to the anti Israel right

conspiracies.claim: Democratic leaders staged absences on purpose to let the Hegseth impeachment die quietly.
conspiracies.status: The absences are on the record. Intent is unproven.
conspiracies.harm: Low to moderate. It deepens distrust between the Democratic base and its leaders just as they take power.
conspiracies.whereSpreading: Consortium News, Antiwar circles, progressive Substacks, Medea Benjamin's campaign against Hakeem Jeffries as Speaker
conspiracies.origin: The Nov 11 House vote to refer the impeachment to committee, 211 to 204, with 11 Democrats absent
conspiracies.whyBelieved: The margin was smaller than the number of absent Democrats, and party leaders have resisted war powers fights before.
conspiracies.caseFor: Eleven named Democrats, including Pelosi, missed a vote whose outcome they could have flipped. Kucinich says leaders owe an explanation.
conspiracies.caseAgainst: No evidence of coordination has surfaced. Absences can be for illness, travel or family reasons, and leaders may prefer a fuller case once the new Congress sits in January.
conspiracies.unknowns: Why each member missed the vote and whether leadership whipped attendance.
conspiracies.watch: Statements from the absent members, and whether impeachment returns as an early item in January 2027.

On the right, Bannon tells the base to drop stolen election talk while Carlson calls Trump's record a betrayal. On the left, Consortium News writers attack Democratic leaders over Hegseth and Israel. items.headline: AP calls Mississippi's Senate race for Democrat Scott Colom
items.summary: The Associated Press called the race for Scott Colom, a Democratic district attorney, over Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith. As of Nov 12 at 5:54pm ET, AP's count showed Colom at 476,120 votes (49.3%) and Hyde-Smith at 470,179 (48.6%), with about 99% of votes estimated counted. Those numbers may have changed since. Mississippi Free Press and WLOX pages carry headlines saying Hyde-Smith conceded and Governor Tate Reeves commented, but we could not open those stories.
items.assessment: A concession would end the county by county court fight that Mississippi's lack of a recount law had set up. Counties still have to certify by Friday, November 13, so watch for any county that misses the deadline.
items.source: Associated Press election results (via results feed), with the concession headline seen on Mississippi Free Press

items.headline: Experian says its data was never meant to check Mississippi voters
items.summary: Mississippi made more than 230,000 voter registrations inactive before Election Day, according to Mississippi Today reporting cited by Newsweek. Many of those voters had to cast affidavit ballots, which are provisional ballots checked later. Experian, the credit bureau whose data was used in the roll cleanup, now says it has not worked for the state since early 2025. It also says its earlier work was not built to validate voter records.
items.assessment: The company has stepped away from the state's process, so Secretary of State Michael Watson now owns the roll cleanup alone. That makes it the obvious first target for the new Democratic Congress and for state lawsuits.

items.headline: About 76% of Mississippi's affidavit ballots were accepted
items.summary: By Tuesday, November 10, counties had processed 15,547 affidavit ballots statewide and accepted about 76%, the secretary of state's office told WLOX. Tuesday was also the last day for mailed ballots to arrive and for affidavit voters to prove their identity at the clerk's office. In Rankin County, a bipartisan committee reviews each ballot before it is opened, so nobody knows the voter's party during the check.
items.assessment: The rejected quarter is now the core of any future case about the Experian roll purge. Each rejected voter is a possible plaintiff, even though the Senate race is settled.

items.headline: House shelves Hegseth impeachment, 211 to 204
items.summary: On November 10 the House voted 211 to 204 to send impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee. That move kills them for this Congress. Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican who lost his primary, filed eight articles. They cover the Iran war, a strike on an Iranian school, boat strikes, the Maduro capture, Yemen and pressure on Senator Mark Kelly. Hegseth called them policy disagreements at his first Pentagon press conference in six months.
items.assessment: Several Democrats were absent, so turnout mattered as much as Republican unity. From January, impeachment is no longer a Republican rebel's move. It becomes a decision Speaker in waiting Hakeem Jeffries must own.

items.headline: Alaska Senate count: Peltola ahead, no AP call before ranked count
items.summary: As of Nov 11 at 10:34pm ET, AP had Democrat Mary Peltola at 121,487 votes (48.9%). Republican Senator Dan Sullivan had 117,512 (47.3%), with about 86% counted. A second, unrelated candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. had 4,100 votes. AP has not called the race and the count is not finished. These numbers may have changed since. Alaska runs its ranked choice count on November 18.
items.assessment: Ballots for the second Sullivan and the other Republican, Gerald Heikes, get passed on to voters' next choices in the ranked count. That makes those small vote totals the thing to watch on November 18.
items.source: Associated Press election results (via results feed)

alsoNoted.headline: Epstein files discharge petition sits a handful of signatures short of 218
alsoNoted.note: A discharge petition is a way to force a House floor vote without leadership. This one would make the Justice Department release more Epstein documents. A second petition, on legal status for people brought to the US as children, is also close. No floor vote was found dated November 10 to 12.

alsoNoted.headline: Warren won't rule out using the December 11 funding deadline to pressure an end to the Iran war
alsoNoted.note: Context: the stopgap now in force, H.R. 6500, passed the House 370 to 48. As of November 3 the House had passed 3 of 12 yearly spending bills and the Senate none (Multibagg summary of Fox reporting). The Fed meets December 8 and 9, two days before the deadline.

alsoNoted.headline: Johnson won't seek a leadership post, and page links report Thune reelected and Jordan chosen as House minority leader
alsoNoted.note: We saw the Thune and Jordan results only as related headlines on the page. Confirm before you use them.

items.headline: US pulls tanker planes out of a British base over an Iran threat
items.summary: On Monday the US Air Force flew at least 10 KC-135 refuelling tankers out of RAF Mildenhall in eastern England. They went to Germany, Spain and Scotland, and Osprey aircraft moved to nearby Lakenheath. The Wall Street Journal tied the move to a threat from Iran, and both bases went to the second highest alert level. The US military would only say it moves aircraft for many reasons.
items.assessment: Iran is now shaping where the US parks aircraft in Europe without firing a shot. Each dispersal costs money and readiness, and it lets Tehran claim its warnings about bases with no geographic limits are being taken seriously.

items.headline: Another tanker hit near Hormuz as an Emirati state ship is damaged
items.summary: A tanker was struck by an unknown projectile about 19 nautical miles northeast of Lima, Oman, on November 10. The crew was safe, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre, a British navy desk that logs attacks on ships. The same afternoon a vessel run by ADNOC, the UAE state oil company's shipping arm, was damaged inside UAE waters. Nobody has claimed either attack.
items.assessment: An attack inside UAE territorial waters on a state owned ship is a step up from hitting foreign tankers in open water. Independent tracking shows Hormuz traffic in single digits a day against about 138 in 2025, while roughly 162 ships wait at anchor off Fujairah.

items.headline: Qatar says Vance may meet Iran's security chief in Doha next week
items.summary: Qatar's prime minister met President Trump for 45 minutes and Vice President JD Vance separately in Washington. Turkey's intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin then said Qatar would host Vance and Iran's top security official Mohsen Rezaei the following week. Tasnim, an Iranian news agency close to the Revolutionary Guards, quoted an official denying any such meeting. The reported deal would ease the US naval blockade and free Iranian funds in exchange for nuclear inspections and a reopened strait.
items.assessment: The leak came from Ankara, not Doha or Tehran, which suggests Turkey wants a visible role as a broker. A public Iranian denial is normal before a first direct meeting, so the denial alone says little. Rough odds of a Vance and Rezaei meeting by month end: about 35%.
items.source: Iran International (citing Al Jazeera and Tasnim)

items.headline: Iran's parliament weighs letting a non cleric run the spy ministry
items.summary: Iran's parliament is preparing to debate a bill that would let someone who is not a cleric head the Intelligence Ministry for the first time. The same bill would let Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei directly appoint the heads of two new bodies inside the ministry. Every intelligence minister since the 1980s has been a cleric.
items.assessment: This would move the spy service further from the elected president and closer to the leader's office and the security forces. It fits a wartime pattern of the new leader pulling security levers toward himself.

items.headline: Iran reportedly names a Quds Force commander as its next envoy to Baghdad
items.summary: Iran has reportedly chosen Abdolreza Masgarian, a commander in the Quds Force, the Revolutionary Guards unit that runs allied militias abroad, as ambassador to Iraq. He would replace Mohammad Kazem Al-e Sadegh. Tehran has not confirmed it. The report came the same day Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi was in Tehran meeting Iran's chief negotiator.
items.assessment: Sending a militia handler as ambassador signals Tehran sees Iraq mainly as a security file. It lands as Baghdad tries to disarm pro Iran factions before a June 2027 deadline set under US pressure.

alsoNoted.note: Zohreh Amiri accused of spreading falsehoods. Opened.

items.headline: New Knesset sworn in as Eisenkot's bloc moves to seize the speaker's chair
items.summary: Israel's 26th Knesset, the parliament, was sworn in on November 10 with no government in place. Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief who leads the Yashar party, has until December 6 to form one, extendable to December 20. His bloc gathered 67 signatures to force a vote next Tuesday replacing Speaker Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally, with Yashar's Matan Kahana. Eisenkot's allies also filed bills for an October 7 state inquiry, prime minister term limits, and repeal of the judicial overhaul.
items.assessment: Winning the speaker's chair would give Eisenkot control of the Knesset agenda before he has a government. That lets him pass the October 7 inquiry and term limit bills even if coalition talks fail, which raises the cost to Netanyahu of forcing a new election.

items.headline: Liberman tells Eisenkot to drop a government backed by Arab parties
items.summary: Avigdor Liberman, leader of the secular nationalist Yisrael Beytenu party, demanded that Eisenkot give up the idea of a minority government kept alive by Arab parties. He says he can bring the ultra Orthodox parties in instead. Those parties have so far said they will not join an Eisenkot government. United Torah Judaism wants written guarantees before any deal.
items.assessment: The math only works one of two ways: outside support from the 19 Arab seats or ultra Orthodox defectors. Liberman's veto blocks the first, and ultra Orthodox demands on the military draft make the second costly. Rough odds Eisenkot forms a government by December 20: about 45%.

items.headline: Raam's Abbas reportedly ready to call Hamas a terror group
items.summary: In the opening session, outgoing Speaker Ohana cited a Ynet report about Mansour Abbas, head of the Islamist Arab party Raam. It says Abbas is willing to call Hamas a terrorist group in talks with the anti Netanyahu bloc. Abbas stood for the national anthem while several Arab lawmakers walked out. A United Torah Judaism lawmaker stood beside him.
items.assessment: If true, Abbas is pricing his support to remove Liberman's main objection to Arab backing. It also splits the Arab lists, since the Joint List is unlikely to match that step.

items.headline: Settlers burn machinery in Beita and beat activists in Qusra
items.summary: Dozens of settlers burned excavators and stone cutting equipment in Beita's industrial zone, south of Nablus, on November 9. The report comes from Palestinian security sources and the WAFA agency. Settlers also beat activists in Qusra and used tear gas on farmers in Beit al-Roush near Hebron. Israeli media said the Beita arson followed Palestinians torching a vehicle near a settlement the day before.
items.assessment: A Palestinian government commission counted 1,369 settler attacks in October, more than double September. Targeting quarry equipment hits one of the few local industries left, which pushes workers toward Israel or out of the area.

alsoNoted.headline: Netanyahu repeats Arab voter fraud claim that election officials found no evidence for
alsoNoted.note: Likud alliance holds 53 seats. Netanyahu cites Iran's nuclear program in his unity pitch.

alsoNoted.headline: Liberman slated to chair the Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, and a first woman lined up to chair Finance
alsoNoted.note: Liran Avisar Ben-Horin of Bennett's party for Finance. Roy Folkman for the Arrangements Committee.

items.headline: Houthis claim a drone hit on Saudi Arabia's Hormuz bypass pipeline at Yanbu
items.summary: On November 11 the Houthis, the Iran aligned group that holds northern Yemen, claimed a drone attack on a pumping station at Yanbu. Yanbu is the Red Sea end of Saudi Arabia's East West oil pipeline, the main route that lets Saudi oil skip the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia reported a limited fire on that pipeline on November 9. The Saudi led coalition says it downed cruise missiles, drones and two ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh the same day.
items.assessment: With Hormuz nearly shut, the East West line is the Gulf's safety valve, and Aramco is planning to expand it. Repeated hits on it would turn the Yemen war into a direct lever on world oil supply.
items.source: WarHistory.org Yemen archive (citing Middle East Eye, LBCI, ISW)

items.headline: Strikes hit Sanaa's gas and oil company sites as missiles hit coalition camps in Aden
items.summary: Strikes on November 10 set gas tanker trailers on fire at the Al-Mafzar station in northern Sanaa. They also hit the Houthi run Yemen Petroleum Company headquarters, according to Houthi media. The Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia, which did not comment. On November 11 police sources told AFP that missiles hit coalition camps in western and central Aden, the seat of the Saudi backed government.
items.assessment: Both sides are now aiming at fuel. That points to a winter fight over heating gas and petrol in Sanaa, and a Houthi push to make Aden unsafe for the government.

items.headline: Houthis close dozens of Sanaa bakeries, raising bread shortage fears
items.summary: Houthi authorities shut dozens of bakeries in Sanaa on November 11, which local sources described as an extortion campaign, according to Arab News. Residents fear bread shortages. It comes as Saudi strikes hit fuel sites in the city.
items.assessment: Squeezing bakers for cash is a sign the Houthi treasury is under strain from the fuel strikes and the blockade. Bread lines in the capital would be the first visible crack in their home front.

items.headline: UN agencies warn over a million in Lebanon face acute hunger
items.summary: The UN Food and Agriculture Organization, the World Food Programme and Lebanon's agriculture ministry warned on November 11 that more than one million people face acute food insecurity. Israeli strikes and shelling continued on the outskirts of southern towns including Markaba, Wadi al-Saluki and al-Jarmaq on November 9, with damage to farmland reported.
items.assessment: The south is Lebanon's farm belt, and shelling of fields keeps it out of production through planting season. That deepens the country's import bill when it has no money.

items.headline: Mada Masr editor's November 11 retrial: outcome not yet public
items.summary: Lina Attalah edits Mada Masr, Egypt's best known independent news site. She was due for retrial on November 11 in a 2024 case that gave her one year in prison in absentia. No outcome had been reported in sources reachable for this edition. Separately, supporters paid her 3 million pound fine, about $55,000, and the appeal against the order closing Mada Masr is set for November 25. The six person staff of Matsadaash, a fact checking group, remain in pretrial detention.
items.assessment: The jailing of Matsadaash's fact checkers shows the target is independent verification, not only one newspaper. The November 25 appeal is the date to watch for whether the closure order is enforced.

alsoNoted.headline: Yemen's army says it has carried out 874 strikes on Houthi positions in Operation Dawn of Yemen
alsoNoted.note: Government says foreign Houthi commanders have been killed. Claim.

Israeli strikes and shelling on southern Lebanon outskirts despite June understandings

items.headline: Abu Dhabi talks end with a prisoner swap deal and no breakthrough
items.summary: Russia and Ukraine agreed in principle on a large prisoner swap after two days of US mediated talks in Abu Dhabi. Russian and US officials announced it on November 11. Russian state news agency TASS says the swap should happen in two to three weeks. Russia's lead negotiator Vladimir Medinsky said the main topic was Europe's future security system, with agreement on some points and not others. On territory he said every inch would return to Russia. Ukraine's negotiator David Arakhamia said a deal by the end of the year is possible and wants Europe at the next round.
items.assessment: The only concrete result is humanitarian, and the core fight over land is untouched. Moscow is steering the talks toward a deal on Europe's security rules, which keeps Europe out and Washington in the middle.
items.source: Al Jazeera; Meduza; The Moscow Times

items.headline: Abu Dhabi day one: talks center on a 1,000 for 1,000 prisoner swap
items.summary: Ukrainian, Russian and US negotiators met for about four hours in Abu Dhabi on November 10. It was their first three way meeting since February. Zelensky said the Russian side proposed swapping 1,000 prisoners each, maybe 1,500 each, and that US officials would carry the offer to Moscow. He said territory came up but must be settled by leaders, not negotiators.
items.assessment: A swap of that size would be among the largest of the war and gives both sides a visible result without touching land. It also lets Moscow show goodwill to Washington while it keeps its Donbas demand intact.

items.headline: Russia brought the FSB officer Kyiv accuses of plotting to kill Budanov
items.summary: Dmitry Minaev runs the counterintelligence operations department of the FSB, Russia's main security service. He sits on Russia's delegation as one of six experts. Ukrainian sources told the Wall Street Journal his department was behind a failed attempt on Kyrylo Budanov, now Zelensky's chief of staff and also at the table. Evan Gershkovich, the freed WSJ reporter, has said Minaev escorted prisoners at the 2024 swap.
items.assessment: Minaev's unit handles prisoner swaps and spy cases, so his presence fits the humanitarian track Moscow wants to lead with. Seating a man Kyiv calls an assassin across from his alleged target also tests how much Ukraine will swallow to keep Washington engaged.

items.headline: US reportedly floated redrawing Donbas borders so both sides can claim victory
items.summary: Meduza's live coverage, citing The Economist, says US negotiators raised changing the official borders of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. The idea would let Russia say it took the regions in full without Ukraine formally giving up land. The same feed cites Axios saying Washington lifted sanctions on Russian diesel sales. Zelensky, speaking from Denmark, said trading Donbas for guarantees is unacceptable without NATO style protection.
items.assessment: If real, the map trick shows Washington looking for wording that hides a concession rather than for a new compromise. Kyiv will likely read the diesel move as a reward handed to Moscow before any result.
items.source: Meduza (live, citing The Economist and Axios)

items.headline: Refinery war forces Russian fuel rationing as Ukraine's grid loses 14 plants
items.summary: Ukrainian drones hit ten Russian oil sites in 11 days, most recently the Kirishi refinery near St Petersburg on November 9. Rosneft, the state oil company, capped sales at 30 liters per car at city stations. Russia carried out more than 130 attacks on Ukraine's power system in a week, and at least 14 of 38 Ukrainian plants are out. Kyiv says it stopped honoring a White House request to spare refineries on October 30.
items.assessment: Each side is trying to arrive at the table holding the other's winter energy hostage, which is why an energy pause was on the day two agenda. Russia's promised diesel shipments to the US have not docked, so Moscow's fuel diplomacy with Washington is weakening just as its home supply tightens.

items.headline: Moscow wants Europe's security rules settled before the Ukraine war
items.summary: Russia's foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said a broad European security framework should be defined before the war itself is resolved, and he rejected a truce. Deputy foreign minister Sergei Ryabkov, who handles arms control, joined the delegation and said it was too early to judge the meeting. Zelensky set the opposite order: stop the war, then guarantees for Ukraine, then wider European security.
items.assessment: Putting arms control people at the table signals that Moscow wants Abu Dhabi to become a talk about NATO in Eastern Europe, not about Ukraine. That framing gives Russia a reason to drag the process out while the front keeps moving.

alsoNoted.headline: Day two agenda: an energy strike pause, Black Sea shipping and a swap
alsoNoted.note: Lists both full delegations. No report of what day two produced was found.

alsoNoted.note: Also says Witkoff and Kushner may go on to Moscow and Kyiv, per Axios.

items.headline: New: Dublin summit will only sketch Europe's Putin envoy, decision in December
items.summary: EU leaders meet informally in Dublin on November 13. They will discuss the profile and mandate of someone to speak for Europe in peace talks, with names coming later. Italy's Giorgia Meloni forced the debate with a letter warning Europe risks irrelevance. Council president António Costa agreed but insists the EU's own institutions must represent it under the treaties.
items.assessment: The quarrel is now less about whether to talk to Putin and more about who controls Europe's voice, Brussels or a big capital. Kushner has said a lasting deal needs direct Russia and Europe talks, so delay until December leaves the US setting the frame alone.

items.headline: EU, US, NATO and Kyiv sign a joint line before facing Russia
items.summary: Before the three way session, the EU, France, Germany, Italy, the UK, Ukraine, the US and NATO met in Abu Dhabi and issued a joint statement. It says any deal must respect Ukraine's borders and give it credible security guarantees. It also says a strong NATO stays central to defending Europe and North America, and that talks should later widen to include Europe.
items.assessment: The text answers Moscow's push for new European security rules by saying Europe's rules should be built on existing institutions, NATO first. Washington signing it limits how far US envoys can trade NATO's future inside the Russia talks.
items.source: Council of the EU statement, summarized by Lovguiden

items.headline: Europe's team waited outside the room in Abu Dhabi
items.summary: The EU sent a joint team led by Björn Seibert, chief of staff to Commission head Ursula von der Leyen. Anna-Maria Boura, a foreign policy adviser to Costa. Security advisers from France, Germany and the UK also came. An EU official said Europeans would not be in the room. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the talks were three way only.
items.assessment: Sending staff chiefs rather than leaders keeps Europe close enough to brief and be briefed, without giving Moscow a chance to refuse a named European face. It also shows the envoy question was not settled in time for this round.

items.headline: Kallas: Europe already has security rules, Russia signed them in 1994
items.summary: EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Russia is only pretending to negotiate, pointing to its air campaign on Ukrainian cities and power plants. She rejected Moscow's call for new European security rules. She said the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, in which Russia, the US and the UK promised to respect Ukraine's borders, already is that framework. France's Jean-Noël Barrot said there can be no European security talks before a ceasefire.
items.assessment: Europe's line is now ceasefire first, while Moscow's is security rules first, so the order of steps is the real fight. Kallas also said she hopes the US midterm results shift Washington, which signals Brussels is planning around a weaker White House.

alsoNoted.headline: European Political Community summit set for Thursday, November 12
alsoNoted.note: Location and outcome not found. G7 foreign ministers also met early in the week, with Ukraine at the top.

alsoNoted.note: Zelensky was in Denmark while his team negotiated.

items.headline: Beijing extends its rare earth pause by just two months
items.summary: China's Commerce Ministry extended its suspension of some export controls to January 10, 2027. The pause had been due to expire November 10. It covers five rare earths, processing technology, some lithium battery and graphite materials, and foreign products containing Chinese rare earths. Controls from April 2025 on seven other rare earths, including dysprosium and terbium, stay in force.
items.assessment: A two month extension keeps Washington and buyers on a short leash through the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and the trade talks after it. Prices for the still controlled metals have already roughly tripled for dysprosium since March, so the pause eases little for magnet makers.
items.source: S&P Global Commodity Insights, Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, Reuters via The Star

items.headline: Beijing confirms talks on a Trump, Putin and Xi meeting at APEC
items.summary: China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said China is in contact with the relevant parties about a meeting of the three leaders. He was responding to a Wall Street Journal report. That report said Xi would only join if the talks allow open discussion of arms control. Guo gave no further detail.
items.assessment: As host, Beijing gets to frame a three way meeting as China brokering between Washington and Moscow. Tying it to arms control lets China look like a peacemaker without having agreed to limits on its own fast growing nuclear arsenal.
items.source: China Ministry of Foreign Affairs, regular press conference

items.headline: No Xi and Takaichi meeting expected at the Shenzhen summit
items.summary: Japanese officials told Jiji Press there will be no summit with Xi on the sidelines of APEC in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19. Beijing still demands that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi retract her 2025 remark that a Taiwan crisis could threaten Japan's survival. China rejected a Japanese offer to reaffirm the 1972 joint statement instead. Asked on November 11, Beijing's spokesperson only said China had made its position clear more than once.
items.assessment: The Taiwan dispute now blocks Japan's top level contact with China for a full year, while Trump meets Xi in the same city. Tokyo risks being the one ally left outside the room if Washington and Beijing strike a deal.
items.source: China MFA briefing (November 11), Jiji Press via The Nation (November 8)

alsoNoted.headline: Beijing calls the Alice Huang spying claims a smear as US lawmakers push chip limits
alsoNoted.note: On November 11 the spokesperson said only that China's position on US chip exports is consistent. See Beijing block for the November 10 denial.

items.headline: Najib goes home under house arrest after a fresh court order
items.summary: Former Malaysian prime minister Najib Razak left Kajang Prison and reached his Kuala Lumpur home at about 9:27 pm on November 10. High Court judge Aslam Zainuddin replaced the November 6 order with a new one based on the conditional royal pardon. The Attorney General's office had held up the earlier order, saying its wording needed clarifying. Najib can serve the rest of his sentence at home until August 23, 2028.
items.assessment: The palace pardon, not the prosecutors, now sets the terms of Najib's punishment. That gives his party UMNO a rallying figure at home and leaves Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim exposed with reform minded voters in his own coalition.

items.headline: Myanmar army says it took an opposition regional headquarters near Yangon
items.summary: State newspaper Myanma Alinn said the army seized a regional command headquarters of the National Unity Government and 10 other bases. The National Unity Government is the shadow government formed by lawmakers the army ousted in 2021. The jungle site is on the Mon and Bago border, about 120 km from Yangon. A Karen National Liberation Army battalion base was also reportedly taken. AP could not confirm the claim.
items.assessment: A win this close to Yangon helps the army's new civilian façade argue it is regaining control before its April 2027 by elections in contested areas. The resistance did not respond, so the scale of the loss is unknown.
items.source: AP via The Star, citing Myanma Alinn

items.headline: Japan gives Vietnam its first security aid and a rare earth pact
items.summary: Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi hosted To Lam, Vietnam's Communist Party chief and president, in Tokyo. They agreed to deepen security cooperation and to cooperate on rare earth metals to make supply chains more resilient. Japan will send its first peacekeeping equipment to Vietnam under its Official Security Assistance program, which gives defense gear to friendly militaries. They also discussed the South China Sea, but announced nothing on it.
items.assessment: Tokyo is building rare earth supply outside China while Beijing keeps its export pause on a two month leash. Peacekeeping gear is modest, but it opens a channel for Japanese defense aid to a country that also fights China over South China Sea claims.

items.headline: Premier Li, not Xi, carries Beijing's trade pitch to Thailand and Manila
items.summary: Beijing said Premier Li Qiang will visit Thailand from November 13 to 15. He will then attend the China and ASEAN summit in Manila on November 15 and 16. ASEAN is the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. China wants an upgraded free trade agreement with ASEAN, called version 3.0, brought into force as soon as possible.
items.assessment: Xi saves himself for hosting Trump at APEC, so Southeast Asia gets the premier and a trade offer while Trump appears in person in Manila. Li arrives in Thailand just after Bangkok tripled its tax on imported electric cars, a move aimed at Chinese brands.
items.source: China Ministry of Foreign Affairs, regular press conference

items.headline: New Zealand's Opportunity Party drops its basic income demand in talks with Luxon
items.summary: Prime Minister Christopher Luxon met Qiulae Wong, leader of the centrist Opportunity Party, on November 9. His coalition holds a majority of just two seats on preliminary counts. Special votes, about a seventh of the total and usually left leaning, are counted by November 27. Opportunity's minimum demands are a stronger competition watchdog, tighter lobbying rules and donation caps. Its universal basic income and land tax ideas are not on the list.
items.assessment: By dropping its signature policies, Opportunity is offering itself as cheap insurance for Luxon. That weakens his right wing partners, ACT and New Zealand First, who are demanding the finance and immigration ministries.

ACT says National keeping the finance ministry is 'no longer tenable'

items.headline: US formally serves India in a lawsuit naming Doval over a murder plot
items.summary: The US State Department served India by diplomatic note in a civil suit filed by Gurpatwant Singh Pannun. Pannun is a US based Sikh separatist who says Indian officials plotted to kill him. The suit names National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and former foreign spy chief Samant Goel. India's foreign ministry called the lawsuit frivolous.
items.assessment: Service by diplomatic note is a routine legal step, but it moves the case toward a ruling on whether India's officials can claim immunity. A loss on that point could expose Indian intelligence methods in a US courtroom.

items.headline: Fake court orders were used to block 129 websites in India
items.summary: Reuters reported that India's telecom department ordered 129 betting websites blocked based on two High Court orders that appear to be forged. The Allahabad High Court filed a police complaint on November 6. Separately, Delhi Police opened a case over forged police notices asking X to block two digital rights groups. Police traced the notices to a 17 year old in Srinagar, and X told a court it would not take the accounts down.
items.assessment: India's blocking system appears to act on paperwork it does not check. That gives anyone with a convincing forgery a way to silence rivals or critics online.

items.headline: Indian inflation tops 6% for the first time in two years
items.summary: Retail inflation rose to 6.09% in October from 5.5% in September. That is above the upper limit of the Reserve Bank of India's target band. Food inflation reached 8.9%, led by onions, garlic and ginger.
items.assessment: The central bank now has little room to cut rates. Food prices this high are politically dangerous ahead of the 2027 vote in Uttar Pradesh, India's most populous state.

items.headline: Assam court says PAN and voter cards alone do not prove citizenship
items.summary: The Gauhati High Court upheld a Foreigners Tribunal order declaring a woman a foreigner. Foreigners Tribunals are special courts in Assam that decide who is an illegal migrant. The judges said a tax ID card and a voter card are issued on self declaration, so they need supporting records. The court also canceled her interim bail.
items.assessment: The papers most poor residents actually hold now count for little in Assam's citizenship cases. That raises the stakes as India's 2027 Census starts collecting identity numbers.

items.headline: Norwegian journalist says India canceled her visa without a reason
items.summary: Helle Lyng Svendsen says India's embassy in Oslo told her not to travel to a summit in Hyderabad. She says her visa was then canceled with no reason given. The Editors Guild of India asked the government to explain and reverse it. The government had not commented.
items.assessment: Screening foreign reporters at the visa stage keeps critical coverage out before it starts. It came the same day the US Embassy in Australia posted a Freedom House map rating India only partly free.

items.headline: Lula leaves for COP31 and Manila, freezing his cabinet picks
items.summary: President Lula flew to Turkey on November 9 for the COP31 climate summit, then goes to Manila for the ASEAN summit of Southeast Asian nations. He returns November 16. He pushed the choice of a 2027 Finance minister and a fiscal adjustment package until after the trip. Allies say he wants names settled by November 25 and the full team announced by December 5.
items.assessment: Markets get about three more weeks with no Finance name, while sitting minister Dario Durigan drafts cuts his successor will inherit. Party bargaining meanwhile sits with Workers' Party chief Edinho Silva, not the presidential palace.

items.headline: Lula wants to tie lawmakers' budget money to their votes
items.summary: Brazilian lawmakers steer a large slice of the federal budget through 'emendas', amendments that fund projects back home. Lula wants to win back sway over part of that money and release it only to those who vote with him. That collides with the budget control now held by Chamber speaker Hugo Motta and Senate president Davi Alcolumbre. No party has agreed to it.
items.assessment: If Lula wins this, his fourth term gets real leverage over a hostile Congress. If he loses, cabinet seats become his only currency, and their price goes up.

items.headline: New: parties that backed Flávio Bolsonaro still bid for Lula's ministries
items.summary: Republicanos, União Brasil and PP endorsed Flávio Bolsonaro, the former president's son, in the runoff. All three still want cabinet posts. PSD is asking for three ministries, including agriculture, and MDB wants to keep its current share. The government now asks each party for a policy plan and an estimate of the votes it can deliver.
items.assessment: Brazil's big centrist parties rent their votes to whoever governs, so backing the loser costs them little. The vote estimate demand is Lula's attempt to price that support before he pays for it.

items.headline: A stronger opposition Senate keeps Lula's senators out of the cabinet
items.summary: Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL) will hold 29 Senate seats and the Novo party 3. Lula's allies are weighing keeping senators Rui Costa, Wellington Dias and Renan Filho in the chamber instead of naming them ministers. Renan Filho was reportedly sounded out to lead the government's bench. Senate president Davi Alcolumbre faces challenges from Rogério Marinho (PL) and Tereza Cristina (PP).
items.assessment: The February 2027 fight for the Senate presidency now matters more to Lula than several ministries. A Senate run by Marinho could stall court nominations and fiscal votes for two years.

items.headline: US report: $12 billion in Venezuelan oil money spent under US control
items.summary: A 53 page State Department report to Congress, dated October 29 and audited by KPMG, covers a US held 'Venezuela Custody Account'. It took in about $12.26 billion from January 3 to September 30, and 98.7% was paid out. Food and consumer goods took 35.75%, administrative services 23%, agriculture 12.5% and health 5.68%. The money came from oil, gold, minerals and fertilizer sales by approved firms.
items.assessment: Washington, not Caracas, now decides how Venezuela's export income is spent, which turns the interim government into a budget client. The vague 23% for 'administrative services' is the line a new Democratic Congress is most likely to probe.

items.headline: Venezuela's Assembly opens the power grid to private generators
items.summary: The National Assembly, led by Jorge Rodríguez, unanimously approved a reform on November 10 letting private firms generate electricity and sell it at a set tariff. It follows new oil and mining laws pushed by acting president Delcy Rodríguez. Opposition deputy Antonio Ecarri backed it, citing the collapse of the state power company. Blackouts hit much of the country daily.
items.assessment: Chavismo is undoing its own 2007 nationalization, and oil fields are the likely first customers, as US Energy Secretary Chris Wright urged in September. Households that now pay almost nothing for power face real bills later.

items.headline: New: Venezuela's army sweeps Apure for armed groups, never naming the ELN
items.summary: Venezuela's armed forces command said on November 12 that units are searching river and forest areas of Apure state for camps and hidden airstrips of 'irregular groups'. The foreign ministry asked for channels with Colombia to share information. Neither statement named the ELN, the Colombian guerrilla group Venezuela bombed days earlier. Two Piaroa Indigenous people were reported killed in ELN and FARC dissident clashes in Bolívar state on November 11.
items.assessment: Caracas is cooperating on paper while avoiding a public break with a group chavismo sheltered for 20 years. Not naming it leaves room to deny a campaign if fighting spreads.

items.headline: ELN frees two investigators after 533 days, then seizes a mayor's wife
items.summary: The ELN guerrilla released two agents of the prosecutor's investigative unit (CTI) in Arauca on November 12, held since May 2025. A day earlier, armed men believed to be ELN abducted Nancy Gómez, wife of the mayor of Uribia in La Guajira. The group also holds army Lt. María Camila Pantoja, taken November 4, and sent proof she is alive. President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered a full deployment to find Gómez.
items.assessment: The ELN swaps old hostages for new ones, keeping bargaining chips as the government's bombing campaign widens. A kidnapping in La Guajira shows it can strike well beyond Catatumbo and Arauca.

items.headline: Fitch puts Paraguay's rating on watch after the Ueno collapse
items.summary: On November 11 Fitch put Paraguay's BB+ rating on watch for a cut and dropped its positive outlook. Ueno, the sixth largest bank, held about $2.9 billion in deposits, and about $2.1 billion of it is uninsured. Roughly $900 million of that belongs to public bodies, including the pension institute and the binational dams. Fitch puts the possible rescue cost at 1.5% of GDP, about $900 million.
items.assessment: The scandal that removed President Peña now threatens Paraguay's long climb toward investment grade. That raises borrowing costs just as the 2027 budget fight starts.

items.headline: Paraguay's pension fund may dip into savings to pay November pensions
items.summary: An internal note at IPS, Paraguay's social security institute, dated November 9 proposes using about 784 billion guaraníes of investment returns to cover November and December payouts. About 411.8 billion guaraníes of its operating cash is frozen at Ueno. The note awaits a legal opinion, and IPS has not commented publicly. The fund already takes in about $72.6 million a month and pays out $73.6 million.
items.assessment: Ueno did not create the hole, it sped it up. IPS actuaries already projected reserves drained by about 2046, and this pulls that date closer.

items.headline: Salvadoran helicopters hit a Haitian gang base, about 20 reported dead
items.summary: President Nayib Bukele said on November 10 that his forces destroyed the headquarters of the 400 Mawozo gang in Croix-des-Bouquets, near Port-au-Prince. He posted video of helicopters firing on the site, and about 20 people were reported killed. Haitian police say they led the raid with Salvadoran support. Amnesty International asked both governments to publish the deployment agreement and allow independent investigations.
items.assessment: Most of Bukele's roughly 2,000 troops are outside the UN backed Gang Suppression Force, so no UN rules bind strikes like this. Prime Minister Fils-Aimé's visit to San Salvador next week will show whether Haiti formalizes or limits the arrangement.

items.headline: Ortega reappears frail after 68 days as Managua rejects Trump's envoy
items.summary: Daniel Ortega appeared on November 9 at a tribute to Sandinista founder Carlos Fonseca, his first public outing since September 2. He walked slowly and gave no speech, and the government has never explained his absences. The independent outlet Confidencial counts 11 appearances this year, against a usual 26. Nicaragua also refused Natasha Franceschi, Trump's ambassador pick, and Washington recalled its chargé d'affaires Elias Baumann.
items.assessment: The recent reform that abolished the vice presidency and created 'presidential designees' now reads as succession planning for co president Rosario Murillo. A US diplomatic downgrade removes one more outside channel during that handover.

items.headline: Sudan lifts its 20 month ban on Kenyan tea
items.summary: Sudan's army led government ended a ban on Kenyan tea imports on November 11. It had imposed the ban about 20 months ago because Nairobi hosted leaders of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the paramilitary it is fighting. The RSF and its allies had signed their parallel government charter in Nairobi.
items.assessment: Port Sudan is using market access to pull Kenya away from the RSF's political wing, and Kenya's tea farmers get a lost buyer back. Watch whether Nairobi now quietly limits RSF political activity on its soil, which would be the real price of the deal.
items.source: Sudan Tribune (via the warhistory.org Sudan event log)

items.headline: Sudanese lawyers doubt the army really arrested ICC fugitive Haroun
items.summary: Ahmed Haroun is a former leader of Omar al Bashir's ruling party wanted by the International Criminal Court for Darfur crimes. AP and Reuters reported on November 8 that the army detained him after a podcast interview. On November 10 and 11 Sudanese politicians, activists and the Emergency Lawyers rights group said there is still no independent proof or official confirmation of the arrest.
items.assessment: A paper arrest would let army chief al Burhan signal distance from Bashir era Islamists to Washington and the Gulf without losing their fighters. If Haroun reappears free, it will confirm that the Islamists, not the generals, set the limits.

items.headline: Hackers drain Kordofan traders' accounts on Sudan's main payment app
items.summary: More than 50 traders and customers in Kordofan say millions of Sudanese pounds vanished from their Bankak accounts. Bankak is the mobile banking app of the Bank of Khartoum. It became the main way Sudanese pay for things after cash ran short during the war.
items.assessment: If people stop trusting Bankak in frontline areas, trade drifts back to cash and informal money brokers, which armed groups find easier to tax and control. It is also a sign that cyber theft is following the war into places with no police to report it to.

items.headline: Congo military court sentences at least 66 soldiers to death for fleeing
items.summary: A military court in Walikale, North Kivu, sentenced at least 66 soldiers to death for cowardice, mutiny and disobeying orders. They were arrested October 20 after reportedly fleeing fighting with the FRN, a rebel coalition that includes M23 and is now led by former president Joseph Kabila. RFI counts 381 death sentences among 507 soldiers convicted since early 2025, though Congo has carried out no formal executions.
items.assessment: With Kabila heading the rebels, the war is now openly about who rules Kinshasa, not only the east. Mass death sentences for retreat may push frightened soldiers to defect rather than run, which is the opposite of what the army wants.

items.headline: Cameroon sets twice delayed elections for February 7
items.summary: President Paul Biya, 93, signed a decree on November 9 setting legislative and local elections for February 7, 2027. Lawmakers' terms were stretched to December 20 and local councilors' terms to February 28. The party of opposition figure Issa Tchiroma Bakary, now in exile in The Gambia, remains suspended. Rights lawyers say up to 2,000 people were detained after last year's election protests.
items.assessment: The local vote matters more than it looks, because municipal councilors elect most of Cameroon's Senate, and the Senate president is the constitutional stand in if Biya dies. Whoever controls these councils shapes the succession to a 93 year old leader.

items.headline: ANC and rivals weigh a bloc to keep the DA out of Johannesburg
items.summary: The Democratic Alliance (DA) won the most votes in Johannesburg, about 35%, but no majority. Bloomberg sources say the ANC, ActionSA, Jacob Zuma's MK party and the Economic Freedom Fighters are discussing an alliance. The goal is to make ActionSA's Herman Mashaba mayor and shut out the DA's Helen Zille. ActionSA chair Michael Beaumont met ANC secretary general Fikile Mbalula on November 8, and parties have 14 days from the results to form councils.
items.assessment: The ANC and DA govern the country together, so a local pact built to block the DA would strain the national coalition. It would also hand Zuma's party a say in the country's richest city.

items.headline: Nine Zimbabweans arrested in Johannesburg over Russia Ukraine war recruitment
items.summary: South African police arrested nine Zimbabweans aged 20 to 26, five at OR Tambo airport and four at a hotel. They are charged under South Africa's law against unauthorized foreign military service. Police have not said which side they meant to fight for or who recruited them, and Zimbabwe says some of its citizens recruited for Russia have died.
items.assessment: After Kenya agreed with Moscow to stop being a recruitment source, the pipeline seems to be shifting to poorer southern African countries using Johannesburg as the transit hub. South Africa's old anti mercenary law is now its main tool against it.

items.headline: Nearly 64,000 Nigerians have fled into Niger this year
items.summary: The UN refugee agency (UNHCR) says nearly 64,000 people fled northern Nigeria for Niger this year to escape Islamist militants and armed gangs. Most went to Diffa and Tahoua, and more than two thirds of those in Diffa are children. Only about 5% are formally registered.
items.assessment: Refugees are fleeing into a military government that has cut ties with Nigeria's regional bloc, which gives Niger's junta a humanitarian card to play against Abuja. It also shows how badly northern Nigeria's security has slipped ahead of the national vote.

items.headline: UNICEF says drone strikes on Sudan's power stations cut off water and care

Drought is making it worse. Its headline called the attacks unlike anything Sudan has seen before. In Rabak, capital of White Nile state, residents have had no electricity for 14 straight days after a drone hit the Mashkour substation, and prices have soared.
items.assessment: Water pumps and hospital fridges need power, so grid strikes work like a slow siege on public health and raise the odds of another cholera wave. Rabak is in army held territory, which points to the RSF, though the reports seen did not name the attacker.

items.headline: Poland says the Pentagon backs a permanent US base Poland will fund
items.summary: Poland's defense minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth gave a green light to a permanent US base at a November 10 Pentagon meeting. Poland offers to pay the building costs, estimated at $3.8 to 4.4 billion, for about 5,000 US troops and up to 25,000 people in total. The White House is expected to decide in early December. All four candidate cities sit west of the Vistula river, far from the Russian and Belarusian borders.
items.assessment: A base deep inside Poland looks more like a rear supply hub than a front line tripwire. That fits Washington's plan for Europe to carry its own conventional defense. Poland is buying a lasting US presence with its own money, a model other eastern allies may copy.

items.headline: NATO now uses Ukrainian forces as the enemy in its drills
items.summary: Adm. Pierre Vandier, who heads NATO's command for future warfare, said the alliance hides Ukrainian troops and Ukrainian sea drones inside its exercises to play the opposing side. The aim is to force NATO units to adapt to cheap drone warfare. Ukraine's defense ministry claims its team beat NATO navies in all five scenarios at a 2025 exercise off Portugal. Breaking Defense could not verify that claim.
items.assessment: A country outside the alliance is now shaping how NATO trains, which gives Kyiv a quiet source of leverage that does not depend on membership. It also gives a non member detailed knowledge of NATO's weak spots.

items.headline: EU agrees its 2027 defense budget as four states refuse to lend to Ukraine
items.summary: The European Parliament and EU governments agreed the bloc's 2027 defense and security budget of about $3.4 billion. It sets aside €650 million for Ukraine from a €90 billion loan pool, while Zelensky has asked for at least €70 billion more. Hungary, Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Bulgaria have opted out of the lending. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz reportedly threatened to block the next long term EU budget if members refuse to chip in.
items.assessment: The group of reluctant payers now reaches beyond Hungary and Slovakia. Merz tying Ukraine money to the next seven year budget turns war aid into a fight over every country's farm and regional funds.

items.headline: Ukrainian missile maker wants SpaceX coverage beyond Ukraine's borders
items.summary: Fire Point, a Ukrainian arms company, wants SpaceX's military satellite network, called Starshield, to work beyond Ukrainian territory. The contract reportedly ends in mid 2027. The firm says its own workaround gives only 15 to 20% of Starshield's capability, a claim not verified. Its FP-9 missile is listed with a range of up to 850 km.
items.assessment: Ukraine's deep strike plans depend on one American company agreeing to switch on coverage over Russia. That makes SpaceX a quiet party to any ceasefire terms on long range strikes.

items.headline: Oil bounces off a ten week low after Trump says no Iran deal is needed
items.summary: Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, hit a ten week low of about $91.5 a barrel on November 10. By November 12 it was back near $96 after President Trump said the US no longer needs a deal with Iran. An Iranian official also ruled out sending enriched nuclear material abroad.
items.assessment: Traders had priced in peace after the midterms, and a single remark reversed part of that bet. Oil is now trading on presidential comments more than on supply, so prices will stay jumpy in both directions.

items.headline: Hotter October inflation lifts December rate hike odds to 87%
items.summary: US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, above the 0.3% forecast. Core prices, which leave out food and energy, rose 0.3%. Futures markets now put the chance of a Federal Reserve hike in December at 87%, up from about 77% a week earlier. The Fed already raised rates in September for the first time in three years.
items.assessment: The war's fuel shock now shows up in the prices the Fed watches most. So a peace deal will not bring quick relief on mortgages and car loans. A rate hike during a tech selloff would squeeze housing markets like Southwest Florida's.

items.headline: Gold slips toward $4,000 during a war, far below its January record
items.summary: Gold traded near $4,050 an ounce on November 10, down from a record above $5,000 in late January. Rising rate hike odds pushed it lower because gold pays no interest. Bitcoin also slid, to about $74,000.
items.assessment: With tankers burning in the Gulf, gold has still lost about a fifth of its value since January. Interest rates now move markets more than fear does, which breaks the usual idea of gold as war insurance.

items.headline: US gas falls below $4, but refiners put off maintenance to get here
items.summary: The AAA national average for regular gas fell to $3.98 a gallon on November 10. Demand dropped after the summer driving season and the switch back to standard time. Many US refineries also delayed routine maintenance this year to keep fuel flowing, and that work will soon come due.
items.assessment: Delayed maintenance is a bill postponed, so many refineries may go offline together in the coming months and tighten supply. Prices under $4 may be a short break rather than a trend.

items.headline: Saudi output jumps 26% as Gulf crude finds ways around Hormuz
items.summary: Saudi Arabia reported a 26% rise in October oil output, and Iraq also raised production. Shipments still depend on other routes and naval escorts. US crude stocks rose by about 4.66 million barrels in the week to November 6, the biggest build since August.
items.assessment: Supply is recovering without any deal, which weakens Iran's main lever of choking the Strait of Hormuz. Any peace would now hit a market that is already well supplied, which would keep prices down.

items.headline: Senate advances a 417 page permitting bill as Trump vows no wind permits
items.summary: On November 9 the Senate advanced a bill to speed permits for data centers, pipelines and power lines. Two Republicans and two Democrats sponsor it, and Trump urged every senator to back it. Trump also said his administration will not approve wind turbine permits, which Politico calls a key part of the bill.
items.assessment: Democrats are being asked to fast track power for AI data centers right after local voters rejected many of them. If wind is shut out in practice, the bill mostly speeds gas and transmission projects.

items.headline: Exxon reaches a preliminary deal to return to Venezuela
items.summary: ExxonMobil, the largest US oil company, has reached a preliminary deal to go back into Venezuela, the New York Times reported on November 9. Exxon was pushed out of Venezuela nearly two decades ago when its projects were nationalized.
items.assessment: Exxon was the major most burned by Caracas, so its return signals that big oil now trusts Venezuelan contracts to hold under the new political arrangement. Other companies are likely to follow if the deal closes.

items.headline: War, not climate policy, pushed global emissions down this year
items.summary: The Global Carbon Budget, an annual scientific tally of carbon dioxide, projects fossil emissions of 32.8 billion tonnes in 2026. That is 0.4% lower than 2025. Oil emissions fell nearly 2% as the Gulf and Ukraine wars drove up fuel prices, while coal emissions rose about 0.6%.
items.assessment: The drop came from a price shock, and rising coal shows some countries swapped fuels instead of cleaning up. When peace makes oil cheap again, emissions are likely to bounce back.
items.source: Carbon Brief daily briefing (citing the New York Times)

items.headline: Pentagon lends $450 million to space firms to cover a coming launch gap
items.summary: The Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital, a lending arm set up in 2022, gave conditional $150 million loans each to Rocket Lab, Stoke Space and LeoLabs. Rocket Lab and Stoke build rockets, and LeoLabs tracks objects in orbit with radar. The loans target a projected shortfall of at least 150 launches through 2030, after SpaceX stops flying commercial payloads on its Falcon 9 rocket in 2028. The office is asking for $20 billion in mandatory funding for 2027.
items.assessment: Both rocket makers are behind schedule, so the Pentagon is backing firms whose new rockets have not flown yet. A defense office lending billions turns the military into an industrial bank with little public debate.

items.headline: UN nature fund for genetic data has raised under $11,000
items.summary: The Cali Fund was set up at the 2024 UN biodiversity summit so companies that profit from genetic data drawn from nature would pay into it. The Financial Times reported it has raised less than $11,000.
items.assessment: Drug, seed and cosmetics firms rely on this data, yet voluntary payments are close to zero. It is a warning for any COP31 climate fund that relies on goodwill instead of binding rules.

items.headline: China hands carbon data to its statistics bureau to fight fake numbers
items.summary: China ordered its National Bureau of Statistics to oversee carbon emission surveys, the South China Morning Post reported. Beijing frames it as part of a push to stamp out fake data using modern technology.
items.assessment: Firmer official numbers could change outside estimates of when China's emissions peak. Better data also strengthens Beijing's hand at a COP31 where the US government sent no official delegation.

items.headline: More than 44,000 tickets issued for passing stopped school buses
